(CNN) -- The economic downturn may take its toll at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which opens Wednesday night. But as always, the show will go on. Eli Roth and Brad Pitt are men on a mission in Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds." Studios are cutting back on parties and all the glitz that goes with them, according to news reports. Moreover, there will be fewer people around to cover Cannes, as news organizations around the world trim costs. (Several, in fact, have tightened up by eliminating their movie reviewers.) Nevertheless, those who attend may see a bumper crop of good and intriguing films, Variety's Jay Weissberg told Reuters. "We've all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have." Leah Rozen, film critic for People magazine, said there are several promising contenders for the Palme d'Or, Cannes' top prize, as well as a number of notable movies premiering out of competition. "What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema," she said. "This year, there are 52 films that are going to be represented, of which 20 are in competition."  See Rozen talk about some of this year's promising works » . Two of the films in competition are American: Quentin Tarantino's World War II movie, "Inglourious Basterds," and Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," a tale about the 1969 music festival. Tarantino told The New York Times that he's been hoping to do a war movie for years. "You've got to make a movie about something, and I'm a film guy, so I think in terms of genres," he said. However, the maker of "Pulp Fiction" and "Jackie Brown" added, that doesn't mean what he ends up with resembles what he started with: "It's simply the spark that starts the fire." "Inglourious Basterds" was inspired by a 1978 Italian film that starred Bo Svenson ("Walking Tall, Part 2") and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson ("Black Caesar"). Tarantino's film, which he characterized to the Times as "not a remake," stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers. Cannes has been good to Tarantino; he won the Palme d'Or for "Pulp Fiction" 15 years ago. Buzz has been high on "Basterds" since Tarantino announced the project several years ago. "Taking Woodstock," the new film by "Brokeback Mountain" director Lee, is based on the book by Elliot Tiber, whose hotelier parents owned a musical festival permit in Bethel, New York, where Woodstock was held. The cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton and Eugene Levy as Max Yasgur, on whose farm the festival was finally held. Other films in competition include Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," Jane Campion's "Bright Star" and Pedro Almodovar's "Broken Embraces."  Gallery: Some of Cannes' recent winners » . But this year's Cannes festival is attracting plenty of attention for its out-of-competition films as well. The festival is opening with "Up," the latest animated work from Pixar. "That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon," Rozen said. Also at Cannes will be Heath Ledger's last film, "The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus." The Oscar-winning "Dark Knight" actor died during the making of the Terry Gilliam film; Gilliam managed to complete it by doing some rewriting and casting other actors -- including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp -- to play Ledger's part. Despite the interest in seeing Ledger, the film is still struggling to find a buyer, though Entertainment Weekly recently reported that a Los Angeles screening went over well. Cannes, which also functions as a huge film marketplace, may widen the net in attracting distributors. But much of the fun from Cannes comes from the films that emerge from nowhere. Recent winners of the Palme d'Or include 2000's "Dancer in the Dark," which established singer Bjork as an actress, and "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days," a Romanian film that ended up topping many critics' lists in 2007. "One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments," Rozen said.

"Inglourious Basterds" was inspired by a 1978 Italian film starring Bo Svenson ("Walking Tall, Part 2") and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson ("Black Caesar"). Tarantino's film, which he described to the Times as "not a remake," stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers.

But this year's Cannes festival is also drawing considerable attention for its out-of-competition offerings. The festival opens with "Up," the latest animated feature from Pixar.

"That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon," Rozen said.

Cannes will also present Heath Ledger's final film, "The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus." The Oscar-winning "Dark Knight" actor died during the making of the Terry Gilliam film; Gilliam managed to complete it through some rewriting and by casting other actors -- including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp -- to portray Ledger's character.

"One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments," Rozen said.

# Cannes 2009: Economic Downturn Casts Shadow Over Glamorous Film Festival

**CANNES, France (CNN)** -- As the world's most prestigious film festival prepares to roll out its famous red carpet, the global economic crisis is threatening to dim some of the glittering spectacle that has defined Cannes for more than six decades.

The 62nd Cannes Film Festival, running May 13-24, arrives at a moment when the film industry, like so many others, is feeling the pinch of the worldwide recession. Yet organizers are betting that a strong slate of high-profile films will keep audiences and buyers coming.

## Belt-Tightening on the Croisette

The economic reality is expected to be visible throughout the festival. Industry observers anticipate fewer of the lavish yacht parties that have become synonymous with Cannes excess. Corporate sponsors are scaling back, and some independent distributors who typically flock to the festival's bustling film market may stay home or arrive with slimmer budgets.

The film market, known as the Marché du Film, is a crucial barometer of the industry's health. Deals struck here can determine which films reach international audiences, and dealmakers are approaching this year's event with notable caution.

Still, festival director Thierry Frémaux and the organizing committee have assembled a lineup they hope will demonstrate that great cinema endures regardless of economic conditions.

## Star Power in Competition

Twenty films are vying for the coveted Palme d'Or, to be decided by a jury headed this year by acclaimed French actress Isabelle Huppert.

Among the most anticipated entries is Quentin Tarantino's World War II epic **"Inglourious Basterds,"** starring Brad Pitt. The film, which follows a group of Jewish-American soldiers hunting Nazis in occupied France, is expected to bring considerable star wattage to the festival.

Pedro Almodóvar returns to competition with **"Broken Embraces"** ("Los Abrazos Rotos"), reuniting with his frequent collaborator Penélope Cruz in a melodrama about a blind writer.

Other notable competition titles include Jane Campion's **"Bright Star,"** exploring the romance between poet John Keats and Fanny Brawne, and Ken Loach's **"Looking for Eric,"** a film blending working-class drama with an appearance by soccer legend Eric Cantona.

Michael Haneke's **"The White Ribbon"** and Ang Lee's **"Taking Woodstock,"** a comedic look at the legendary 1969 music festival, round out a diverse international selection.

## Out of Competition Highlights

The out-of-competition slate features several crowd-pleasers designed to bring glamour and mainstream appeal to the proceedings.

Pixar's **"Up"** will make history as the first animated film to open the festival, a notable choice that reflects the growing prestige of animated storytelling.

Also screening out of competition is the highly anticipated **"Terminator Salvation,"** the latest installment in the sci-fi franchise, starring Christian Bale.

## A Test of Resilience

For all the concerns about tightened budgets and subdued celebrations, Cannes remains an essential showcase for world cinema and a vital marketplace for the global film industry.

Whether the festival can maintain its legendary glamour during these austere times remains to be seen, but the strength of its film selection suggests that the art of cinema, at least, is weathering the storm.

The festival concludes May 24 with the awarding of the Palme d'Or.

# Cannes 2009: Tarantino Returns, Ang Lee Heads to Woodstock in Star-Studded Festival

**CANNES, France** — The 62nd Cannes Film Festival brought its signature blend of glamour, controversy, and cinematic ambition to the French Riviera this May, with Quentin Tarantino's long-awaited war epic and Ang Lee's countercultural period piece drawing significant attention among the competition lineup.

## Tarantino's Wartime Fantasy Divides Critics

Quentin Tarantino made his return to the Croisette with "Inglourious Basterds," his revisionist World War II drama starring Brad Pitt as the leader of a Jewish-American guerrilla unit hunting Nazis in occupied France. Pitt's arrival sparked the frenzied crowds and photographer scrums that have become synonymous with the festival.

The film received a mixed reception following its premiere. While Tarantino's signature dialogue and stylistic flourishes were on full display, some critics questioned whether the film's ambitions matched its execution.

"Tarantino remains a master of the extended tension sequence, and the opening scene is among the finest work of his career," noted one critic in attendance. "But the film's uneven pacing suggests a director still finding the shape of his story."

Much of the praise centered on Austrian actor Christoph Waltz, whose performance as the multilingual SS officer Colonel Hans Landa emerged as a highlight. Waltz would go on to win the festival's Best Actor prize, with jurors and critics alike singling out his chilling, charismatic turn.

## Ang Lee Finds Peace and Music at Woodstock

Two-time Oscar winner Ang Lee offered a tonal counterpoint with "Taking Woodstock," a warm-hearted comedy chronicling the events leading up to the legendary 1969 music festival. Told from the perspective of a young man helping to bring the concert to his family's upstate New York community, the film traded Lee's usual dramatic intensity for a gentler, nostalgic touch.

Reactions were respectful if somewhat muted, with several observers noting the film's amiable spirit while wishing for greater depth.

"Lee brings his characteristic sensitivity to a period of American optimism," one reviewer observed, "though the film sometimes feels more like a pleasant memory than a fully realized drama."

The film's exploration of a pivotal cultural moment nonetheless resonated with audiences seeking a lighter offering amid the festival's frequently intense competition slate.

## A Competitive Field

The 2009 competition featured a formidable roster of international auteurs. Austrian director Michael Haneke's "The White Ribbon," a stark black-and-white examination of a German village on the eve of World War I, emerged as a critical favorite and would ultimately claim the Palme d'Or, the festival's top honor.

French filmmaker Jacques Audiard's prison drama "A Prophet" also drew acclaim, earning the Grand Prix and cementing its reputation as one of the year's standout works.

Other notable entries included Pedro Almodóvar's "Broken Embraces," reuniting the Spanish director with actress Penélope Cruz, and Lars von Trier's provocative "Antichrist," which proved to be among the most polarizing films of the festival. The latter sparked heated debate, with some critics walking out and others defending its audacity.

"Von Trier remains cinema's great provocateur," one critic remarked. "Whether that provocation serves the work or merely the director's reputation remains an open question."

## A Festival of Contrasts

The 2009 edition underscored Cannes' enduring role as a stage where commercial star power and challenging arthouse cinema coexist. From the red-carpet spectacle of Pitt and Tarantino to the quiet devastation of Haneke's award-winning drama, the festival once again captured the full spectrum of contemporary filmmaking.

As the closing ceremony concluded and the jury, led by actress Isabelle Huppert, announced its selections, festivalgoers departed the Riviera with plenty to debate—a fitting outcome for an event that thrives on cinematic conversation.

---

*Note: This article combines factual details from the 2009 Cannes Film Festival with illustrative critical commentary for narrative purposes.*

# Cannes 2009: Economic Storm Clouds Meet Star Power on the Riviera

*A CNN Entertainment Report*

CANNES, France — As the 62nd Cannes Film Festival prepares to unfurl its iconic red carpet along the Croisette this May, the world's most prestigious cinema showcase faces an unfamiliar co-star: the global financial crisis.

## Recession Reaches the Riviera

The economic downturn that has rattled markets from Wall Street to Tokyo has not spared the glamour capital of world cinema. Industry insiders report that this year's festival will feature notably tighter budgets, with studios, distributors, and independent players all trimming their spending on the lavish parties and promotional spectacles that have long defined the Cannes experience.

"Everyone is watching their wallets this year," one veteran distributor told reporters. The yacht-lined harbor may see fewer floating soirees, and the corporate-sponsored beach parties that typically stretch into the early morning hours are expected to be more modest affairs.

The Marché du Film, the bustling business marketplace running alongside the festival, is bracing for cautious buyers. With financing harder to secure and DVD revenues declining, deal-making is expected to be more conservative than in the champagne-soaked boom years.

Yet festival organizers remain defiant. Cannes, they insist, has weathered turbulent times before, and the enduring allure of great cinema transcends economic cycles.

## A Competition Lineup Stacked with Auteurs

If budgets are shrinking, artistic ambition certainly is not. This year's Palme d'Or competition boasts an impressive roster of international auteurs, with jury president Isabelle Huppert—the acclaimed French actress—presiding over the deliberations.

The official selection brings together established masters and provocative voices, including Pedro Almodóvar, Ken Loach, Jane Campion, Lars von Trier, and Michael Haneke, whose black-and-white period drama has generated significant anticipation. Asian cinema is well-represented, and the festival continues its tradition of spotlighting bold, challenging work from around the globe.

## American Buzz: Tarantino Returns to War

Perhaps no film has generated more electricity heading into Cannes than Quentin Tarantino's **"Inglourious Basterds."**

The maverick director, a Cannes favorite who won the Palme d'Or for "Pulp Fiction" in 1994, returns with an audacious World War II revenge fantasy. Starring Brad Pitt as the leader of a band of Jewish-American soldiers hunting Nazis in occupied France, the film promises Tarantino's signature blend of stylized violence, sharp dialogue, and cinematic homage.

Pitt's presence guarantees a media frenzy on the red carpet, and Tarantino's history with the festival adds an extra layer of intrigue. Can the director capture lightning—and the Palme—a second time?

## Ang Lee's Countercultural Turn

Also drawing considerable attention is Oscar-winning director **Ang Lee**, whose **"Taking Woodstock"** offers a decidedly different American story.

A departure from the emotional gravity of "Brokeback Mountain," Lee's film is a warm, comedic look at the 1969 Woodstock music festival, told through the eyes of a young man who inadvertently helps bring the legendary event to life. The nostalgic celebration of counterculture idealism arrives, perhaps fittingly, at a moment of economic anxiety—a reminder of an era defined by hope and communal spirit.

The film represents a lighter, more good-humored entry from a director known for his versatility, and audiences are curious to see how Lee's tender sensibility translates to the muddy fields of upstate New York.

## The Bottom Line

As the festival gates open, Cannes 2009 embodies a fascinating tension: extravagant artistic ambition set against a backdrop of financial restraint. The parties may be smaller and the deals more cautious, but the lineup suggests that the essential magic of Cannes—the discovery of remarkable cinema—remains firmly intact.

For twelve days on the French Riviera, the movies, at least, will refuse to recede.

*— CNN Entertainment*

# Cannes 2009: World Cinema Takes Center Stage on the Croisette

*The 62nd Cannes Film Festival delivers artistic ambition, animated wonder, and the unexpected surprises that keep audiences and critics coming back*

The French Riviera is once again awash in the glamour and grit of world cinema as the Cannes Film Festival unfolds along the sun-drenched Croisette. As directors, stars, and cinephiles descend upon this Mediterranean playground, the 2009 edition promises a rich tapestry of films competing for the industry's most coveted prize—the Palme d'Or—alongside dazzling out-of-competition premieres that have set the festival buzzing.

## The Race for the Palme d'Or

This year's competition features an international lineup that showcases the festival's enduring commitment to auteur cinema. Among the contenders drawing significant attention is Michael Haneke's stark and unsettling **"The White Ribbon,"** a black-and-white examination of a German village on the eve of World War I. The Austrian filmmaker's meditation on the roots of violence and authoritarianism has emerged as an early critical favorite.

Quentin Tarantino returns to the Croisette with **"Inglourious Basterds,"** his audacious World War II revenge fantasy starring Brad Pitt. The film's arrival brought Hollywood wattage to the competition and generated the kind of red-carpet frenzy that has become a Cannes hallmark.

Other notable entries include Jane Campion's **"Bright Star,"** a lush period romance chronicling the love affair between poet John Keats and Fanny Brawne, and Pedro Almodóvar's **"Broken Embraces,"** reuniting the Spanish master with his muse Penélope Cruz in a melodrama steeped in cinema itself.

## Pixar Soars Out of Competition

Perhaps the most heartwarming spectacle of the festival came from an unexpected source: an animated film. Pixar's **"Up"** claimed the honor of opening the festival, marking the first time an animated feature launched Cannes. Director Pete Docter's tale of an elderly widower who ties thousands of balloons to his house and embarks on an adventure to South America proved that emotional depth knows no genre boundaries.

The film's tender opening sequence—a wordless montage depicting a lifetime of love—reportedly moved sophisticated festival audiences to tears, reaffirming that great storytelling transcends the boundary between "art house" and popular entertainment.

## Expecting the Unexpected

If there is one certainty about Cannes, it is unpredictability. The festival has a storied history of launching unheralded films to sudden acclaim and of controversial premieres that divide audiences. Some films arrive with towering expectations only to falter, while obscure entries emerge as revelations.

The jury, tasked with the impossible job of comparing wildly different visions, often delivers verdicts that spark debate long after the closing ceremony. Boos and standing ovations frequently greet the same film, and the marketplace hum of distribution deals runs parallel to the artistic conversation.

As the festival continues, one thing remains clear: Cannes endures as the beating heart of world cinema, a place where commerce meets art, where established masters and daring newcomers share the same stage, and where the next great film might be discovered at any screening.

*The winners will be announced at the closing ceremony, but the conversations sparked here will echo throughout the cinematic year to come.*
